“I don't think anyone would even notice if I stopped coming,” Lalremsiami said, eyes on the cracked tiles of the bus stop.
“Oh come on, you say this every exam week.”
“No, I mean it this time. I can't sleep and I don't want to eat.”
“You're exaggerating, Lali. Seriously. Did you finish the maths sheet?”
“Uma, I—”
“The bus is so late. Did you see what Nisha posted?”
Uma told herself it was only a bid for attention from her friend, and that if it were real, Lalremsiami would have said it differently. Lalremsiami looked at her, nodded slowly and pulled her scarf higher. The counsellor's room was two floors above them, and neither mentioned it. On the bus they sat side by side without a word, and Lalremsiami got off two stops early.

qa.q: Where were Uma and Lalremsiami when they talked?
qa.a: They were at the bus stop, and the counsellor's room was two floors above them.

qa.q: What was Uma thinking when she changed the subject?
qa.a: Uma thought it was only a bid for attention, and she probably felt uncomfortable, so she turned to the maths sheet and the late bus.

qa.q: What could Uma try instead, and why?
qa.a: Uma could ask what Lalremsiami means, listen, and offer to walk with her to the counsellor upstairs, because not sleeping, not eating and saying nobody would notice deserve to be taken seriously.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami likely feel after the talk?
qa.a: More alone: she pulled her scarf higher, stayed silent on the bus and got off two stops early.

grounding: A teen tells herself her friend is exaggerating and changes the subject, missing the chance to link her with help.

I still think about that Tuesday. I'm Rekha. Suraj and I were walking back from tuition at five when he said, quietly, “Sometimes I feel like I'm just done with everything.”
And I thought: here we go. Suraj always made things sound bigger than they were. So I said, “You're so dramatic,” and started talking about the chemistry test. He went quiet and didn't mention it again.
At seven, a message: “forget what I said. shouldn't have said anything.” I could almost see his face, like I'd closed a door on him, which I had.
It kept bothering me through dinner. What if it wasn't drama? What if he'd tried to tell the one person he trusted, and I'd changed the subject? I told Mummy everything right there at the table. She didn't lecture; she called Suraj's mother that minute, and his mother went to sit with him. The next morning she took him to the school counsellor.
I'd wasted my first chance. I nearly wasted the second.

qa.q: What did Suraj say on the walk back from tuition?
qa.a: Sometimes I feel like I'm just done with everything.

qa.q: What did Rekha think when Suraj said it?
qa.a: Rekha felt irritated and dismissive, thinking Suraj was being dramatic again, and changed the subject.

qa.q: What could Rekha have said on the walk instead?
qa.a: Something like "That sounds serious, tell me more," and then helped Suraj reach a trusted adult that same day.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt after being called dramatic?
qa.a: Suraj likely felt dismissed and more alone, which is why he messaged to take it back.

grounding: Shows a teen dismissing a friend's worrying words as drama and changing the subject, leaving him more alone and nearly missing the chance to get him help.

Teacher's note, Friday, after lunch duty
At lunch I was on duty near the back benches and overheard part of a conversation. Wasim, who has been unusually quiet this month, said to Gargi, “Honestly, nobody would care if I didn't come back after the holidays.” Gargi laughed, said, “Stop fishing for attention,” and turned to ask someone about the cricket score. Wasim put his head down on the desk and stayed like that.
I don't think Gargi meant to hurt him; she looked uncomfortable, as if she didn't know what else to say. But the moment passed with nobody taking it seriously, and he looked more alone afterwards than before.
I did not wait. I took Wasim to the counsellor's room during sixth period, and the counsellor phoned his father before school ended. Afterwards I spoke to Gargi quietly: what he said deserved a pause, not a joke, and bringing it to an adult is never snitching.

qa.q: What did Gargi say to Wasim?
What might Gargi have been feeling when she laughed it off?
qa.a: Gargi looked uncomfortable and unsure, perhaps nervous about what to say, so she turned it into a joke.

qa.q: What could Gargi do if a friend says something like this again?
qa.a: Pause, ask what the friend means, and bring a trusted adult in the same day instead of changing the subject.

qa.q: What was the moment like for Wasim?
qa.a: Wasim put his head down and seemed more alone, having reached out and been laughed at.

grounding: A teacher notes a teen dismissing a friend's worrying words as attention seeking and changing the subject, leaving him more alone, before stepping in.
